title: What do you do?
goals: Say and ask what a person does for a living (He's an engineer, What do you do?).
Use a, an, the or no article correctly with jobs and other nouns.
Talk about your family and other people's families (my cousin's dad is a police officer).
Express possession with have/has, 's and possessive pronouns (mine, yours, hers…).
Write a short paragraph about a relative using capital letters and periods correctly.
Describe jobs and people's qualities (well-paid, hardworking, rewarding).

words.example: My aunt is a doctor in a small clinic.
A taxi driver knows the city very well.
His dad is a police officer.
A singer needs a good voice.
They're actors in a TV show.
My brother wants to be a designer.
His mom is a piano teacher.
His dad is a police officer.
I have two brothers and a sister.
His grandparents' house is near the school.
My mom's dad is my grandfather.
My mom has a sister: she's my aunt.

learn.title: Articles: a / an / the / no article
learn.html:
English needs an article with a job in the singular: for example, He is a doctor. With plural nouns, we don't use a/an.

CaseRuleExample
aSingular, starts with a consonant sounda teacher, a singer, a university student
anSingular, starts with a vowel soundan actor, an engineer, an architect
no article (–)Plural in general, or general ideaswriters, students, lawyers; English teachers help students
theSomething already mentioned, or unique / known to everyonea school… The school is in Boston; the government, the internet

Count the sound, not the letter: an hour, but a university.

watch.why: A job in the singular takes a/an.
Lawyer starts with a consonant sound.
The article is also needed in negative sentences.

watch.wrong: A school is in Boston. (ya mencionada)

learn.title: Possession with have / has
learn.html:
Used to say what people have (family, objects). With he / she / it we use has.

AffirmativeNegativeQuestionShort answer
I/you/we/they have a laptopI/you/we/they don't have a laptopDo you have a laptop?Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
He/she/it has a brotherHe/she/it doesn't have a brotherDoes she have a brother?Yes, she does. / No, she doesn't.

After doesn't and does, the verb goes back to have.

watch.why: After doesn't, the verb goes back to have.

learn.title: Possessive 's and s'
learn.html:
Shows who owns something or who is related to whom. The order is the reverse of Spanish: the book of Laura = Laura's book.

SituationFormExample
Singularname + 'smy mother's best friend, Tom's parents
Regular plural (ends in -s)name + 'my grandparents' house, your parents' jobs
Irregular plural (doesn't end in -s)name + 'sthe children's teacher
Family by last namethe + last name in the plural + 'the Smiths' address

Careful: 's can also mean is (Max's a sound engineer = Max is) or show possession (Max's dad). The context makes it clear.

watch.wrong: The house of my parents is big.
watch.why: In English, the owner goes first.
children is an irregular plural: add 's.

learn.title: Possessive adjectives and pronouns (+ Whose)
learn.html:
They avoid repeating the noun. The adjective goes before the noun; the pronoun replaces it.

SubjectAdjective (+ noun)Pronoun (alone)
Imy (name)mine
youyouryours
hehishis
sheherhers
weourours
theytheirtheirs

Whose asks who owns something: Whose is the pen? — It's Matt's. / It's his.

watch.why: Without a noun after it, use the pronoun.
Before a noun, use the adjective.
hers, his, yours, ours and theirs don't take an apostrophe.

learn.title: Capital letters
learn.html:
Used to write with correct spelling. English uses more capital letters than Spanish.

CapitalizedExample
Start of a sentenceShe writes stories.
The word I, alwaysMy sister and I are doctors.
Names of people and titles with namesMr Daniels
Cities, towns, statesTexas, London
CountriesPeru, Mexico
Languages and nationalitiesEnglish, Spanish, French
Days of the week and monthsWednesday, November

At the end of a sentence, put a period (.).

watch.why: Languages take a capital letter (in Spanish they don't).
I always takes a capital letter.
Days of the week take a capital letter.

words.example: Job security matters to my father.
I love working for the government.
He feels lonely in a new city.

learn.title: Useful expressions
learn.html:
• What do you do? / What does he do? — asking about a job.
  • I'm a… / He's an… — saying what your job is.
  • Where do you work? — asking where someone works.
  • … is my cousin / my mom's sister. — introducing a family member.
  • He/She loves his/her job because… — giving your opinion about a job.
  • It's a well-paid / rewarding / challenging job. — describing a job.
  • Whose is this? — It's mine / yours / hers. — asking and saying who something belongs to.
  • He has a big family. / She doesn't have kids. — talking about your family.

practice.instructions: Choose or write the correct article (a, an, the), or show that there is no article.

items.prompt: My cousin is ___ electrician in Monterrey. (a / an / the)
items.explain: Electrician starts with a vowel sound → an.
Plural jobs: no article.

items.prompt: I need ___ umbrella today. (a / an / the)
items.explain: Umbrella starts with a vowel sound → an.

items.prompt: We live in Puebla. ___ city is beautiful. (a / an / the)
items.explain: We already mentioned the city (Puebla) → the.

items.prompt: Is your uncle ___ accountant? (a / an / the)
items.explain: Accountant starts with a vowel sound → an.

items.prompt: She is ___ university student. (a / an / the)
items.explain: University starts with a /ju/ sound (consonant) → a.

items.prompt: Please close ___ door, it's cold. (a / an / the)
items.explain: It's a door both people know → the.
Plural jobs: no article.

practice.title: Possessives: write the correct form

items.prompt: my brother (the car of) → It's my ___ car.
items.explain: Singular: name + 's.

items.prompt: the children (the toys of) → These are the ___ toys.
items.explain: Children is an irregular plural: 's.

items.prompt: my grandparents (the house of) → This is my ___ house.
items.explain: Regular plural ending in -s: just an apostrophe.

items.prompt: Ana (the phone of) → ___ phone is new.

items.prompt: This backpack belongs to me. It's ___.
items.explain: No noun after it: pronoun mine.

items.prompt: Those keys belong to you. They're ___.
items.explain: Pronoun for you: yours.

items.prompt: The tickets belong to Rosa and me. They're ___.
items.explain: Rosa and me = we → ours.
Miguel = he → his; Miguel's is also correct.

write.prompt: Write 5 or 6 sentences about a relative of yours: their name, how they are related to you, how old they are, what they do for a living, where they live, and whether they like their job and why. Use a/an, 's and has, and check the capital letters and periods. Starter example: Lupe is my aunt. She's…
checklist: Name and relationship (Lupe is my aunt.)
has with he/she (She has two kids.)
Capital letters for names, cities, countries and languages, and for I
A period at the end of each sentence
5 to 6 sentences, with a subject in each one
write.model: Lupe is my aunt. She's my mom's sister, and she's 45 years old. She is an engineer, and she lives in Puebla, Mexico. She has two kids and a small dog. She likes her job because it is interesting.

reading.title: My family in Puebla
reading.intro: Read Laura's text about her family and answer.
paragraphs: Hi! My name is Laura and I'm from Puebla. I have a small family. My parents are Javier and Rosa. My dad is a taxi driver. My mom is an English teacher. Her job is challenging, but it's rewarding.
My brother's name is Diego. He is a software engineer in Mexico City, and he has a good salary. His wife is Karen. She is a doctor. They have two children, a son and a daughter.
My mom's sister is my aunt Carmen. She doesn't have children, but she has three dogs. Her husband, Pedro, is a firefighter. It's a dangerous job, but he loves it.
My grandparents' house is big. We have dinner there on Sundays. Is your family big or small?

listening.title: A photo of the family
listening.intro: Listen to Elena and Ricardo talk about a photo. You can repeat the conversation.

lines.text: Ricardo, is that your brother in the photo?
Yes, he is. His name is Jorge. He's a lawyer.
A lawyer! Does he have a family?
Yes, he does. He has a wife and a daughter. His wife is an architect.
Nice! And your parents? What do they do?
My dad is a doctor, and my mom is a journalist. They're very hardworking.
What about you? What do you do?
I'm a designer. It's a creative job, and I love it.
That's great. Oh, is this phone yours?
No, it isn't mine. It's my brother's.
